Chance
chans
n. (an occurrence without apparent cause; used by the Philistine diviners as a hypothesis, by the Preacher as an observation, and by our Lord in a parable — never by Scripture as an explanation)
From Latin cadere, to fall, through Old French cheance, a falling out — the same root as cadence and accident. The Hebrew at 1 Samuel 6:9 is miqreh, a happening, from qarah, to befall; the Greek at Luke 10:31 is sugkuria, a coincidence.

Biblical Definition

Scripture uses the word, and never as an ultimate account of anything. The Philistine priests devise a test for the ark and state the alternatives exactly: if the kine go up to Bethshemesh, the LORD did this; “but if not, then we shall know that it is not his hand that smote us: it was a chance that happened to us” (1 Samuel 6:9). The kine went straight up, lowing as they went, turning aside neither to the right hand nor to the left — and chance was excluded by an experiment the pagans designed themselves. The Preacher observes what appears from below: “the race is not to the swift, nor the battle to the strong… but time and chance happeneth to them all” (Ecclesiastes 9:11) — the phrase under the sun governs the whole book, and it describes the view from ground level, not the truth about heaven. Our Lord says “by chance there came down a certain priest that way” (Luke 10:31), using the ordinary human idiom in a parable to mean the priest had no plan to be there. And a young Amalekite says he happened by chance on mount Gilboa (2 Samuel 1:6) — in a speech Scripture shows to be a lie.

Webster 1828 Definition

Webster (1828) defines chance as an event that happens without being designed or expected, and observes that in reality there is no such thing, since every event has a cause.

expand to see more

CHANCE, n. An event that happens, falls out or takes place, without being contrived, intended, expected or foreseen; the effect of an unknown cause, or the unusual or unexpected effect of a known cause; accident; casualty; fortuitous event.

In strictness of speech, chance has no existence; there is no such thing as an event without a cause.

2. Fortune; what fortune may bring; as, they must take their chance.

3. An event, good or evil; success or misfortune; luck.

CHANCE, v.i. To happen; to fall out; to come or arrive without design or expectation.

Key Scripture

1 Samuel 6:9 — "And see, if it goeth up by the way of his own coast to Bethshemesh, then he hath done us this great evil: but if not, then we shall know that it is not his hand that smote us: it was a chance that happened to us."

Ecclesiastes 9:11 — "I returned, and saw under the sun, that the race is not to the swift, nor the battle to the strong, neither yet bread to the wise, nor yet riches to men of understanding, nor yet favour to men of skill; but time and chance happeneth to them all."

Luke 10:31 — "And by chance there came down a certain priest that way: and when he saw him, he passed by on the other side."

Proverbs 16:33 — "The lot is cast into the lap; but the whole disposing thereof is of the LORD."

Modern Corruption

Chance has been promoted from a description of human ignorance into a metaphysical cause — a thing that explains outcomes rather than confessing that we do not know them.

expand to see more

Webster saw the point clearly in 1828: in strictness of speech, chance has no existence; there is no such thing as an event without a cause. The word properly names a limit in the observer, not a power in the world. Modern usage has quietly made it a cause — things happen by chance, and the phrase is offered as an explanation that closes the question. It explains nothing. To say an event occurred by chance is to say one does not know why it occurred, which is often a perfectly honest thing to say and is never a rival account to providence. The Reformed doctrine does not deny contingency as men experience it; it denies that contingency is ultimate.

Proverbs 16:33 is the decisive text and it is deliberately provocative: the lot is cast into the lap; but the whole disposing thereof is of the LORD. The lot was the ancient world's purest instance of randomness, and Scripture assigns its outcome entirely to God — which is why the lot fell on Jonah, why the land was divided by lot, and why Matthias was chosen by it. Ecclesiastes 9:11 is not a contradiction but a report from under the sun: from ground level the swift lose races and the wise go hungry, and no pattern is visible. Both are true. The believer lives with the second and rests in the first.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Hebrew miqreh, a happening — 1 Samuel 6:9, Ecclesiastes 9:11; qarah, to befall; Greek sugkuria, coincidence — Luke 10:31; goral, a lot — Proverbs 16:33.

expand to see more

Hebrew miqreh — an occurrence, a happening; 1 Samuel 6:9 and Ecclesiastes 9:11.

Hebrew qarah — to befall, to meet; the root of miqreh.

Hebrew goral — a lot; Proverbs 16:33, whose disposing is of the LORD.

Greek sugkuria — a coincidence, a chance meeting; Luke 10:31, its only New Testament occurrence.

Latin cadere, to fall — the root of chance, cadence, and accident.

Usage

"“It was a chance that happened to us” — a hypothesis the Philistines tested and disproved."

"“Time and chance happeneth to them all” — the view under the sun."

"“The whole disposing thereof is of the LORD” — of the lot, the purest randomness known."
